citation.authors: Buch, E.R., Young, S., & Contreras-Vidal, J.L.
citation.title: Visuomotor Adaptation in Normal Aging

study.eligibility_rationale: Upper-extremity visuomotor rotation reaching task comparing young and elderly adults, with data during exposure (late adaptation) and after removal of the distortion (aftereffects), reported in English. "Visuomotor adaptation to a gradual or sudden screen cursor rotation was investigated in healthy young and elderly subjects." and "Finally, trials 401–440 (40 trials; 10 per target direction) were performed with normal visual feedback to test for aftereffects (post-exposure condition)."
study.design_notes: Between-subjects design on two factors: age group (young, elderly) and distortion type (gradual, sudden). "Both age groups were equally divided at random into two subgroups", so the sudden and gradual contrasts involve DIFFERENT participants and are two independent datasets (5 per cell from 10 elderly and 10 young). No participant experienced more than one distortion type and there was only a single round of adaptation (pre-exposure 40 trials, exposure 360 trials, post-exposure 40 trials), so all data come from first exposure. No contextual change between the exposure and post-exposure phases: the same four targets, same hand and apparatus were used throughout ("The start position and all four targets were visible throughout the entire duration of the testing session"), only the cursor rotation was removed. Note that post-exposure feedback was normal (veridical cursor) rather than withheld — the aftereffect is the first post-exposure trial (and the mean of the first four), which the authors argue is "free of volitional strategic shifts". Two dependent measures are reported for each outcome (standardized IDE and standardized RMSE); both are z-scores relative to each participant's own pre-exposure mean/SD. Per-subgroup Ns and per-subgroup ages are never printed separately; ages are given only for the full groups of 10 (elderly 73.3 ± 6.70 yr, young 21.00 ± 2.70 yr). Figure 2's caption ("10 traces total per target direction for each condition" from two trials per subject) is consistent with 5 subjects per cell. No numeric group means/SDs appear in the text for late exposure or aftereffects; those values are only plotted in Figures 3 and 4.

datasets.chosen_pair_rationale: Only two age groups exist (elderly = Group A, young controls = Group B); within the sudden distortion condition the elderly subgroup is paired with the young subgroup. The gradual subgroups are different participants and form a separate dataset, not an alternative pairing.

moderators.perturbation_size_deg: 90° CCW screen cursor rotation from the onset of exposure

outcomes.measure_name: Standardized initial directional error (IDE) score, z-score relative to pre-exposure (one of two measures reported; RMSE is recorded separately)
outcomes.units: standardized score (z-score of IDE in degrees, relative to pre-exposure mean/SD)
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: In terms of performance, gradual adaptation resulted in less directional and spatial errors, but reduced aftereffects, whereas step adaptation resulted in normal aftereffects, but increased spatial variability during adaptation.
outcomes.operationalization: Late-exposure under the sudden 90° CCW rotation: "we used the Kruskal-Wallis test to compare the means of the trial-blocks during the adaptation to the 90° rotation (e.g., late-exposure)"; trial blocks are means of four consecutive trials, and IDE is z-scored against each subject's pre-exposure mean and SD. Fig. 2C plots an alternative operationalization (normalized shift of initial movement direction, in degrees, over the last two/five trials of exposure).
